A window with no row of its own for an antenna and feed (a -1 row beside rows for other windows, or no row at all, as for ALMA's WVR window) leaves that cache entry untouched: receptorAngles_p is resized to the same shape, which casacore's Array::resize does not reinitialise, so receptorAngles() gives the previous window's angles (or, for the first window iterated, zeros: the new array's elements are value-initialised). XRADIO 1.3.1's converter makes the same per-dataset choice and writes such a dataset with no receptor angles. casa-rs reads an antenna and feed's rows in the window, else its rows for every window, and states no receptors where it has neither. Where FEED's rows are all -1 or all name windows, which is how CASA's simulator, ALMA and casa-rs's MSv2 writer write it, the receptors are the same.

docs.title: spw "no match" warnings refuse the expression
docs.text:
• Date noted: 2026-11-02
  • Status: CASA behaviour casa-rs follows for parity (#980, casa-ms selection::spw_expr)
  • Affected code: casacore ms/MSSel/MSSSpwErrorHandler.h, MSSelection.cc (initErrorHandler, setErrorHandler)

MSSSpwErrorHandler only logs its reports (handleError posts a WARN), so a spw term matching nothing (0,7 on a 4-window MeasurementSet, an unknown name) looks meant to be a warning. But it does not override clone(), and MSSelection installs mssEH->clone(), a base MSSelectionErrorHandler, which throws: CASA 6.7.6.14 refuses 0,7 with "Spw Expression: No match found for 7," (resources/casa-compat/evidence/msselection-spw-casa-20261102.json). casa-rs refuses it too.

docs.title: A spw frequency range with a negative step can loop forever
docs.text:
• Date noted: 2026-11-02
  • Status: CASA bug casa-rs does not follow (#980)
  • Affected code: casacore ms/MSSel/MSSpwIndex.cc (matchFrequencyRange)

A stepped window range f0~f1^s with s < 0 steps by each window's least CHAN_WIDTH, in single precision. A window whose widths are negative then steps away from f1 and never leaves the loop; a step too small to move a single-precision frequency stalls it. CASA 6.7.6.14's ms.msselect does not return for 4GHz~5GHz^-1MHz on a MeasurementSet with a descending window (not_returning in the evidence file). casa-rs refuses such expressions.

docs.title: spw channel quirks casa-rs follows
docs.text:
• Date noted: 2026-11-02
  • Status: CASA quirks casa-rs follows for parity (#980)
  • Affected code: casacore ms/MSSel/MSSpwIndex.cc, MSSpwParse.cc, MSSpwGram.yy

A single window frequency (1.4GHz) matches a window within its largest signed CHAN_WIDTH of the window's midpoint, so never a window whose widths are negative. A channel range in hertz reads the channel order from the sign of the first CHAN_WIDTH, not from the frequencies. When a window's first frequency channel range finds no channel, selectChannelsFromIDList skips one range instead of the window's ranges, so the next window takes the skipped window's later ranges (0~2:4.5GHz~4.55GHz;0~1 gives window 2 the ranges 0~1 and -1~63). In a window list, a frequency replaces the list but not its write position (100GHz~101GHz;0 lists the matched windows, then window 0). ( ... ) skips endOfCeremony, so the expression keeps every MAIN row. All are in the evidence file; casa-ms reproduces them, and tclean refuses the parenthesized form and a window kept without channels, whose imaging in CASA is not established.

docs.title: A tuned cube selection compares outframe frequencies with LSRK ones
docs.text:
• Date noted: 2026-11-03
  • Status: CASA bug casa-rs does not follow (#980, casa-imaging-application compile::frequency_bands)
  • Affected code: casatools synthesis/ImagerObjects/SynthesisImagerVi2.cc (selectData, andFreqSelection), SynthesisImager.cc (tuneSelectData), CubeMajorCycleAlgorithm.cc (task)

A cube is gridded by CubeMajorCycleAlgorithm's own SynthesisImagerVi2. Its selectData states each channel range spw names as a frequency band in tclean's outframe (MSUtil::getFreqRangeInSpw over the range's channel centres at every time of the window's rows) and stores it in freqBegs_p and freqEnds_p. Where tuneSelectData tunes the selection (the first visibility buffer's window has 30 or more channels, or the model is saved to MODEL_DATA), it calls selectData again with the image's band, pixel −1.5 to nchan + 0.5, in LSRK, and andFreqSelection narrows each stored band that band overlaps to their intersection, without converting either: a band in TOPO or BARY numbers is intersected with one in LSRK numbers, and the result is read as LSRK (FrequencySelectionUsingFrame(LSRK)). The two frames differ by up to tens of km/s, so with channels narrower than that, an image whose band overlaps the stored one in those numbers loses the image's edge channels (or gains channels CASA never meant to read) at every time. The same andFreqSelection narrows two of a window's own channel ranges to their intersection when a Doppler shift across the track makes their bands overlap, which keeps almost nothing of either. casa-rs states a tuned selection's bands in LSRK before intersecting them with the image's, and keeps each named range's band whole; with outframe='LSRK', the default, and ranges further apart than the shift, the selections agree. No case of CASA's test suite reaches either difference: the one tuned cube with channels narrower than the shift, test_cube_D2, images in LSRK, where casa-rs and CASA select the same channels at every time (its edge plane keeps 2460.56 of 5020.51 in both).

docs.title: A cube's fine frequency grid lets rounding choose one or two samples per plane
docs.text:
• Date noted: 2026-11-03
  • Status: CASA rounding casa-rs does not follow (#980; test_cube.test_cube_5 differs by it)
  • Affected code: casatools synthesis/TransformMachines2/FTMachine.cc (interpolateFrequencyTogrid)

For linear interpolation onto planes wider than a channel, CASA places floor(width) points per plane, with width the ratio of the plane spacing (imageFreq_p, from the image's spectral coordinate and its LSRK conversion layer) to the visibility buffer's first channel spacing (its channels converted to LSRK by the visibility iterator). Where planes are a whole number of channels wide, the ratio is that number exactly at the image's epoch, and after it the Doppler shift moves it by about 1e-6, below or above. test_cube_5 (refim_point.ms, 50 MHz TOPO channels, width='100MHz', outframe='TOPO') has a ratio of 2 at its first integration: the image's epoch is that integration's time and its direction the field's to the last bit, and the shift then lowers the ratio below 2 at every later integration, where both implementations place one point per plane. At the first integration CASA's two conversions round apart and its ratio falls below 2, so it places one point there too; casa-rs's ratio is 2 to rounding and it places two. Every plane of casa-rs's cube therefore holds the first integration's weight twice: its sum of weights exceeds CASA's by exactly that integration's share of the track, 0.0017154 (the rows of one of its 480 integrations, unflagged, over all), and its PSFs differ by 7e-4 to 1.3e-3 normalized RMS, the returned maxpsfsidelobe by 3e-4. Which side of 2 a ratio that is 2 exactly falls on is rounding, which casa-rs does not reproduce (AGENTS.md: a near-tie broken the other way is equally valid).

docs.title: A cube without a per-channel density leaves <imagename>.gridwt behind
docs.text:
• Date noted: 2026-11-03
  • Status: CASA behaviour casa-rs does not follow (#980; test_onefield.test_onefield_pcwdT_and_pcwdF.2's inventory differs by it)
  • Affected code: casatools synthesis/ImagerObjects/SynthesisImagerVi2.cc (runCubeGridding), SynthesisImager.cc (getWeightDensity, setWeightDensity), SIImageStore.cc (gridwt), CubeMajorCycleAlgorithm.cc (task)

A cube weighted by Briggs or uniform weighting with perchanweightdensity=False forms one VisImagingWeight density in the imager defining the cube. To hand it to the CubeMajorCycleAlgorithm imagers that grid the cube, runCubeGridding asks getWeightDensity, which writes the density grid to a new paged image <imagename>.gridwt and passes its name in the control record (weightdensity); each gridding imager reads it back with setWeightDensity. Nothing removes the file. A later run into the same name forms its density again and overwrites it, and reads the file only for the shape of an image store that has no other product (SIImageStore's constructor, whose comment there asks "How can this be right ?"). Its pixels are a uv-plane density, but its coordinates are the image's sky coordinates, with a FIELD_ORDER axis added for several fields. casa-rs forms the density once and grids with it in the same process, so it writes no such file; CASA 6.7.6.14 writes tst2.gridwt in test_onefield_pcwdT_and_pcwdF's second call, whose other products agree.

docs.title: W projection grids a support the grid's edge cuts, and never its last row and column
docs.text:
• Date noted: 2026-11-03
  • Status: CASA behaviour casa-rs follows for parity (#980, casa-imaging-operator GridEdge::Sectioned)
  • Affected code: casatools synthesis/TransformMachines2/WProjectFT.cc (put), FTMachine.cc (findGridSector, tweakGridSector), synthesis/fortran/wprojgrid.f (sectgwgridd, sectgwgrids, onmywgrid, sectdwgrid, owp)

WProjectFT::put grids through the sectioned sectgwgridd: each sector findGridSector cuts grids the taps of a sample that fall on it and adds weight · Σ Re(cwt) over those taps to sumwt, wherever the sample's anchor lies (onmywgrid asks only that the support meet the sector). A support that overruns the grid is therefore gridded in part and weighed by the part, where the unsectioned gwgrid and the degridder (sectdwgrid through owp) drop it. The sectors start at the grid's first column and row (both findGridSector and tweakGridSector add one to the 0-based start, giving the 1-based x0 = 1, and onmywgrid clips a support's low end to it), and findGridSector cuts the last one short (nxsub = nxp - x0 - 1 before that increment), so they cover every column and row but the grid's last: no tap lands before the grid, and the last column and row are never gridded, though owp predicts a support that reaches them. casa-rs grids the taps on the sectors and weighs them, as CASA does. Dropping the whole sample, as casa-rs did, left test_cube_wproj_onefield's 1.5 and 1.8 GHz planes (refim_oneshiftpoint.mosaic.ms, four planes, whose supports overrun the grid at those frequencies) short of CASA's sumwt by 3.06 and 14.57 and their PSFs 3.6% and 5.3% apart in normalized RMS; they now agree with CASA 6.7.6.14 to 8e-7. (An earlier reading of the sectors as starting at the 0-based column 0, so that a tap one column below the grid would be written before it and weighed, mistook findGridSector's start before its final increment for the start it returns.)

docs.title: A CRTF spectral range rounds each end to a channel, toward zero
docs.text:
• Date noted: 2026-11-03
  • Status: CASA quirk casa-rs follows for parity (#980)
  • Affected code: casatools imageanalysis/Annotations/AnnRegion.cc (_extend), casacore images/Regions/WCBox.cc (doToLCRegion), lattices/LRegions/LCBox.cc

A region's range=[f1, f2] masks the channels from Int(p1 + 0.5) to Int(p2 + 0.5), where p1 ≤ p2 are the ends' pixels on the image's spectral axis. Int truncates toward zero, then the low end is clamped to 0 and the high end to the last channel. A region whose ends cross is left out, and the other regions are kept. Because of the truncation, a range ending up to 1.5 channels below the cube masks channel 0, while one starting half a channel above it masks nothing. An MFS image's one channel is its whole bandwidth wide. casa-rs follows this, measured with CASA 6.7.6.14 on refim_point.ms's cube and MFS image: rg.fromtext and tclean's .mask for 20 ranges, in the unit test compile::domains::tests::a_spectral_range_masks_the_channels_casa_masks.

docs.title: A mask string of several lines is an empty mask in tclean
docs.text:
• Date noted: 2026-11-03
  • Status: CASA bug casa-rs corrects (#980)
  • Affected code: casatools synthesis/ImagerObjects/SDMaskHandler.cc (reading mask text)

CASA 6.7.6.14's tclean given mask='circle[[50pix,50pix],10pix]\nbox[[10pix,10pix],[12pix,12pix]]' makes an empty mask and stops at code 7 without cleaning. The same regions as a list, or as lines of a region file, mask both regions. casa-rs reads every line of the text as a region of the mask, as the list and the file read.

docs.title: tclean checks a vis list for repeats of its first entry only
docs.text:
• Date noted: 2026-11-03
  • Status: CASA bug casa-rs corrects (#980)
  • Affected code: casatasks private/mslisthelper.py (check_mslist), called by ImagerParameters.checkAndFixSelectionPars

CASA 6.7.6.14's tclean refuses vis=['a.ms', 'a.ms'] with "a.ms is contained in the list more than once." (ValueError, before any imaging). The check compares each later entry with the first one only, after the list is sorted by time, and as text. So ['a.ms', 'b.ms', 'b.ms'] and ['a.ms', './a.ms'] pass it, and their samples are read twice. The message states the evident intent: no MeasurementSet twice. casa-rs refuses any repeat, comparing canonical paths, with CASA's message. Evidence: CASA's refusal of [refim_point.ms, refim_point.ms] on the oracle host, 2026-11-03, and the T1 law vis_list::a_measurement_set_named_twice_is_refused.

docs.title: A common beam's circular case is the reciprocal of its axis
docs.text:
• Date noted: 2026-11-03
  • Status: CASA bug casa-rs corrects (#980)
  • Affected code: casatools imageanalysis/ImageAnalysis/CasaImageBeamSet.cc (_transformEllipseByScaling, used by getCommonBeam)

_transformEllipseByScaling computes a scaled ellipse's axes as c1 = sqrt(1/k1) and c2 = sqrt(1/k2). When they are exactly equal, a circle, it returns sqrt(k1) for both axes instead: the reciprocal of the axis. That contradicts the general branch and the function's evident intent. casa-rs returns the axis. Both take the circle branch only for exactly equal axes, which scaling rarely produces. An earlier casa-rs absolute tolerance of 1e-12 took sub-arcsecond beams in radians for circles of the reciprocal axis, about 3e6, and the common-beam search then never ended. casa-rs works in radians where CASA works in arcseconds; the common beams agree within one of the algorithm's 0.1% growth steps (casa-numerics law the_common_beam_of_sub_arcsecond_beams_is_found_whatever_the_unit).

Situational guidance for agents: read only the section relevant to the task.

docs.title: CASA And C++ Oracles
docs.text:
• Local CASA task runs use the CASA 6.7.6 release's Python, /Applications/CASA.app/Contents/MacOS/python3, which has casatasks and casatools. Scripts take CASA_RS_CASA_PYTHON to use another one. On the Mac mini the release (6.7.6.14) is /Volumes/Extra Storage (not encrypted)/DeveloperTools/CASA.app, so set CASA_RS_CASA_PYTHON to its Contents/MacOS/python3 there.
  • The CASA task inventory (resources/casa-compat/casa-6.7.6.14/) is pinned to CASA 6.7.6.14. scripts/test-casa-inventory.sh compares it with the installed CASA and fails when CASA is missing or another version; --write re-records it and regenerates docs/reference/casa-compatibility.md.

docs.title: plotms PNG Export
docs.text:
For headless CASA plotms oracle PNGs, set:

DISPLAY=${DISPLAY:-:99}
QT_QPA_PLATFORM=${QT_QPA_PLATFORM:-offscreen}
MPLBACKEND=${MPLBACKEND:-Agg}

Then call casaplotms.plotms with showgui=False, plotfile=..., expformat="png", and overwrite=True.

The local macOS CASA build does not use Xvfb, but plotms still requires DISPLAY. Do not run this CASA/Qt path in a shell sandbox that blocks sysctl CPU-feature queries: Qt may mis-detect arm64 NEON and print Incompatible processor. Use the normal user environment or an explicitly unsandboxed command runner.

docs.title: Shared Data Roots
docs.text:
TESTING.md is the canonical resolver policy. Current workstation locations are:

  • Shared CASA C++ test data: CASA_RS_TESTDATA_ROOT, ../casatestdata, or ~/SoftwareProjects/casatestdata; long-gate preflight may select /Volumes/home/casatestdata when it contains the required paths.
  • Tutorial parity data: CASA_RS_TUTORIAL_DATA_ROOT/tutorial-parity/... or ~/SoftwareProjects/casa-tutorial-data/tutorial-parity/.... No copy is kept; /Volumes/home/casa-rs/tutorial-data/ holds the download scripts and checksums to fetch the data from NRAO.
  • Measures runtime data: an explicit root supplied to MeasuresRuntime::open, or a complete CASA_RS_MEASURESPATH / ~/.casa/data candidate selected by the application before opening the runtime. Discovery never installs data.
  • Small bundled real-MS CI fixtures: crates/casa-ms/tests/fixtures/.

Slow, release, parity, and tutorial gates run shared-data preflight and report the selected root. Do not use /private/tmp as a canonical dataset location or add personal workstation archives as implicit default-gate fallbacks.

docs.title: Storage Locations
docs.text:
Follow the storage rules in AGENTS.md. Current locations:

  • Internal disk (small; keep at least about 40 GB free): source, builds, and small durable evidence for quick tests under /Users/brianglendenning/SoftwareProjects/casa-rs-evidence/<work-item>/.
  • NAS storage over Tailscale, mounted at /Volumes/home: large or long-lived artifacts under /Volumes/home/casa-rs/. Shared CASA test data is at /Volumes/home/casatestdata. The laptop mounts it at login and remounts it when it drops (a user LaunchAgent; the login is in the Keychain).
  • External disk GLENDENNING at /Volumes/GLENDENNING/: a 1 TB NVMe SSD (about 3 GB/s), fast working space for large datasets and runs, never the only copy of anything that matters. Copy a run's inputs onto it from the NAS first; never read a large MeasurementSet over the network in place.
  • Archives of earlier GLENDENNING disks on the NAS, each with a README.md that maps its paths: /Volumes/home/casa-rs-glendenning-preserve/GLENDENNING/ and /Volumes/home/casa-rs/glendenning-stick-20261016/.

Keep an MS or large output only when it will be reused and would take hours to regenerate: a fixed timing input, or a long CASA run used as a correctness reference, kept with the exact MS it ran on. Record its generator, parameters and timings in a manifest beside the archive (for example T55's casa-rs-evidence/t55/GOLDEN-DATASETS.md in the preserve archive).

docs.title: Workstation Toolchain
docs.text:
• Keep Xcode and the Command Line Tools on the same major version. If cc links fail with tapi error ... unknown architecture (for example while building fitsio-sys), xcrun is resolving a newer Command Line Tools SDK than Xcode's linker understands: update Xcode, or set SDKROOT=$(xcode-select -p)/Platforms/MacOSX.platform/Developer/SDKs/MacOSX.sdk.
  • After an Xcode update, run sudo xcodebuild -license accept and sudo xcodebuild -runFirstLaunch; until then git and cc fail.
  • FFTW: casa-fft finds FFTW through pkg-config, so a plain build links Homebrew's FFTW, which has no NEON kernels. Releases build the SIMD FFTW with scripts/build-fftw.sh. Performance work and timing evidence use the same build: on this workstation it is PKG_CONFIG_PATH=/Users/brianglendenning/SoftwareProjects/fftw-3.3.11-simd/lib/pkgconfig. Check which FFTW a binary linked (the target/release/build/casa-fft-*/output link path, or nm BIN | grep -c n1fv_ for NEON codelets) before comparing timings, and link both sides of an A/B against the same FFTW.

docs.title: Cloud Sessions
docs.text:
Claude Code cloud sessions run in a Linux container prepared by .claude/hooks/session-start.sh. Variables in the cloud environment's settings extend it; a session reads them when it starts.

  • TS_AUTHKEY joins the session to the owner's tailnet in the background (.claude/hooks/tailscale-up.sh; log in /var/log/tailscale-up.log). Use an ephemeral key. The container has no UDP, so peers are reached through Tailscale's relays: fine for SSH and small files, slow for bulk data.
  • CASA_RS_MAC_SSH_KEY lets the session work on the Mac mini (bg-mac-mini) as the owner: the macOS-only crates and Metal tests, the CASA oracle, or a second build beside the local one. scripts/mac-run.sh COMMAND mirrors the working tree to the mini and runs COMMAND there (--help for details).
  • The value is a private key without a passphrase whose public half is in the owner's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the mini, base64-encoded onto one line (base64 -i KEY | tr -d '\n' on macOS). CASA_RS_MAC_USER overrides the login name (default brianglendenning).
  • Copies live in ~/ext/SoftwareProjects/casa-rs-cloud/src/<branch>/ on the mini (the top of the ~/ext volume is owned by root) and share one target/ beside src/; CASA_RS_MAC_ROOT overrides the location. Remove a branch's copy with scripts/mac-run.sh --clean once its work is merged or pushed.
  • Commands run in a login shell, which reads ~/.zprofile and ~/.zshenv but not ~/.zshrc; settings the tests need, such as CASA_RS_MEASURESPATH, belong in the former. ~/.zshenv must print nothing, or rsync fails with "is your shell clean?". Stopping the script does not stop the command at once; it ends when it next writes output.
  • The script uses Homebrew's rsync on the mini when it is installed and the system openrsync otherwise; if openrsync refuses a transfer, brew install rsync there.
  • Run work that reads large data on the mini, next to the NAS and GLENDENNING, and bring back only results.
  • The NAS is not mounted in cloud sessions: the container's kernel has no SMB support and the NAS needs its own login. Reach its data from the mini, which does not mount it by default: the owner mounts it there (Finder or screen sharing) when a run needs it, and SSH logins see it under /Volumes while it stays mounted. Non-public datasets stay off the cloud container (AGENTS.md).

docs.text:

  • Local installs: just install-local (or just install-local-suite)
  • Release install: just install-release <version>

docs.title: Imaging Evidence
docs.text:
TESTING.md ("Imaging tiers and evidence") says what an evidence run must record. Locations on this workstation:

  • T1.5 harness (not in the repository): working copies at /Volumes/GLENDENNING/casa-rs-evidence/if/IF-8/{refim,kernels}, each with t15.py, casa_references.py and its data/, casa/ and bin/ folders.
  • Staging: restage them on GLENDENNING from the NAS before a run:
    • the scripts and the CASA 6.7.6 references from the t15-*.tar archives in /Volumes/home/casa-rs/if10/;
    • the inputs from the NAS casatestdata (measurementset/{vla,alma,evla}, unittest/tclean).
  • Running: run T15_TAG=-<commit> /Applications/CASA.app/Contents/MacOS/python3 t15.py bin/casars-imager-<commit> [cases] in each folder, with a binary built from the committed state; both take about 15 minutes.
  • A jumped result: check the case's image.summary.json backend. A case that names no backend runs on auto.
  • T2 matrix: tools/perf/imager/run_workload.py with CASA_RS_IMPERF_DATA_ROOT set to a staged copy of the inputs on GLENDENNING (casa-rs-imperformance, from its NAS mirror) and CASA_RS_CASA_PYTHON.
  • Receipts: write them under /Volumes/GLENDENNING/casa-rs-evidence/if/t2/, then archive them to the NAS.
  • CASA oracles: casa-rs/if10/t2-oracles-20261013.tar and casa-rs/glendenning-stick-20261016/casa-oracles-and-inputs-20261013-14.tar.
  • Timed rows and large inputs (pilot, 512-plane cube, deep32, full cube, Wave3, #625): ~/SoftwareProjects/casa-rs-if10-data.noindex/ on this laptop, ~/ext/SoftwareProjects/casa-rs-data/ on the Mac mini, and the NAS manifests under /Volumes/home/casa-rs/if10/.
  • Wave3: the MS that CASA's Wave3 reference was imaged on is casa-rs/glendenning-stick-20261016/wave3-regenerated-ms-20261013.tar, not the differing original in the NAS mirror.
  • Baseline: the pre-refactor build f38033668a is the baseline for diagnosing a regression, not for accepting a row.
  • An explicit memory policy: production reads none from the environment. An evidence run that needs one (forced paging, a fixed budget) builds an evidence-only patch of ImagingRequest::resource_policy and HostResources::detect from the committed head, labels the binary with the patch, and reverts the checkout afterwards; IF-11's patch is recorded on #660.

docs.title: Calibration Tasks User Guide
docs.text: This guide shows how to run the casa-rs calibration tasks from the calibrate command line and from Python.

docs.title: The calibration surfaces
docs.text:
All calibration work runs through one provider executable, calibrate. The application catalog exposes it as these task surfaces:

  • calibrate: the general surface; --mode selects apply, export_corrected_data, fluxscale, gencal, solve_bandpass, solve_gain, stats, or summary
  • gaincal, bandpass, applycal, fluxscale, gencal: CASA's tasks, with CASA 6.7.6's parameters, defaults and values

Every surface is a one-shot task. Run it as calibrate <surface> (calibrate bandpass --ms ...; calibrate alone is the general surface), which resolves a parameter profile (Defaults, Last, Last Successful, or a TOML file), applies overrides, saves Last state in the workspace, and runs the task. See Task Parameter Profiles for sources and managed Last files, and the generated parameter reference for every parameter and its CLI flag.

Use a writable copy of the dataset when you intend to apply calibration, because applycal (and calibrate --mode apply) writes CORRECTED_DATA in place, as CASA's does. As in CASA, a calflag run first saves the flags to the next applycal_N flag version (flagbackup, default on), so flagmanager can restore them; --no-flagbackup skips it, and calonly and trial change no flags and save none.

docs.title: ngc5921.ms walkthrough
docs.text:
Expected field roles:

  • field 0: flux/bandpass calibrator
  • field 1: phase calibrator
  • field 2: target

Recommended reference antenna: VA15.

workdir=$(mktemp -d /tmp/casars-cal.XXXXXX)
cp -R /path/to/casatestdata/measurementset/vla/ngc5921.ms "$workdir/ngc5921.ms"
cd "$workdir"
  1. Solve a phase-only gain on field 0:

bash calibrate gaincal --vis ngc5921.ms --caltable ngc5921.G0 \ --refant VA15 --gaintype G --calmode p --solint inf \ --field 0 --spw 0 --smodel 1,0,0,0

  1. Solve the bandpass on field 0, applying the gain table on the fly:

bash calibrate bandpass --vis ngc5921.ms --caltable ngc5921.B0 \ --refant VA15 --gaintable ngc5921.G0 --field 0 --smodel 1,0,0,0

  1. Apply both tables to field 0:

bash calibrate applycal --vis ngc5921.ms \ --gaintable ngc5921.G0,ngc5921.B0 --field 0

  1. Inspect the solutions and the corrected data with calibrate --mode stats or --mode summary, and plotms.

The CASA-named surfaces take CASA's chain: the --gaintable list, with the positional --gainfield, --interp and --spwmap lists, so the i-th table takes the i-th entry of each and a table past the end of a list takes CASA's default (every field, linear, no window map); --calwt gives one flag for every table or one per table. A flag's value is split at commas, so an entry that holds a comma, such as CASA's interp='nearest,linear', is given as a Python list: --interp "['linear', 'nearest,linear']", and so is a window map per table: --spwmap '[[0, 0], []]'. --docallib --callib FILE applies a CASA calibration library instead. --applymode trial reports the apply plan without changing the MeasurementSet. calibrate --mode apply keeps casa-rs's own --gaintables with ;-separated per-table lists.

CASA's empty smodel solves against the MODEL_DATA column where the MeasurementSet has one and a 1 Jy point source where it does not; bandpass does not solve against MODEL_DATA yet, so give it a point source. CASA reads a field's virtual model (setjy with usescratch=False) before MODEL_DATA; casa-rs does not yet, so an empty smodel on a MeasurementSet that holds one is refused. A CASA parameter casa-rs does not implement yet is taken only at its default, and a CASA value it does not implement yet (such as gaintype='K') is refused; both refusals name #979. docs/reference/casa-compatibility.md lists them.

Use calibrate gaincal --template to see every parameter with its default, and --save-params FILE to keep a run's resolved profile for reuse with --params FILE.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
The same surfaces are generated functions under casars.tasks with CASA's signatures (casars.tasks.gaincal(...), casars.tasks.applycal(...), and so on), returning what CASA's tasks return, and casars.tasks.run("gaincal", ...) accepts the same parameters and returns the run's TaskCompletion. Each call starts the calibrate executable in the current directory (or in tasks.run's workspace), passes its log to sys.stderr, and saves no Last. CASA's parameters are the consent; there are no separate confirmations.

from casars import tasks

solved = tasks.gaincal(vis="ngc5921.ms", caltable="ngc5921.G0", refant="VA15",
                       gaintype="G", calmode="p", solint="inf", field="0", spw="0",
                       smodel=[1, 0, 0, 0])
solved["selectvis"]["antennas"]   # the antennas the solve selected

Profiles saved before these surfaces took CASA's names load as the runs they meant: out_table becomes caltable, gain_type='g' becomes gaintype='G', the ;-separated per-table lists become CASA's positional lists, and so on. Where CASA's default differs (applycal's calwt, gaincal's calmode and smodel, bandpass's combine and smodel), a profile that left the value out adopts CASA's default with a warning.

overwrite=True replaces only the -o report today. A run that would write a calibration table or MeasurementSet that already exists is refused whatever overwrite says: gaincal, bandpass and gencal caltables, the fluxscale table, and the corrected-data export. Choose a new name, or remove the old product first. Bringing these in line with CASA, whose gaincal replaces an existing caltable, is #945.

docs.title: Current limitations
docs.text: • there is not yet a dedicated setjy task

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
casa-rs supports an installer-driven suite install on macOS arm64 and Linux x86_64.

The installer published with each release:

  1. downloads the matching suite bundle
  2. installs it into a versioned suite root
  3. creates a suite-local Python environment from the bundled wheel
  4. updates the stable/rc channel links, and links the suite's task executables into ~/.local/bin

That keeps the task executables and the Python package behaving as one installed suite: the suite's Python starts the executables in its own suite's bin/.

docs.title: macOS prerequisites
docs.text:
Install the Apple command-line tools and a supported Python:

xcode-select --install
python3 --version

Release wheels are built for Python 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12.

docs.title: Install a stable release
docs.text:
Choose the version you want to install:

version=0.15.0
curl -fsSL "https://github.com/bglenden/casa-rs/releases/download/v${version}/install-casa-rs.sh" \
  | bash -s -- --version "$version"

That creates:

  • ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>
  • ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/stable
  • ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/current
  • for each task executable in the suite's bin/, such as calibrate, msexplore, imexplore, mstransform and casars-imager: ~/.local/bin/<command> and ~/.local/bin/<command>-stable

feather, immath and impv are not linked into ~/.local/bin, and there is no split command: they are CASA names that are also system commands (split is a coreutil) or generic words. Run split as mstransform split; Python starts all of them from the suite's bin/. A link in ~/.local/bin that points into the install root but no longer resolves, such as one to a command a newer suite does not have, is removed. A file of your own, or a link elsewhere, already at one of these names is left in place, and the installer says so.

docs.title: Install a release candidate side by side
docs.text:
Release candidates use the same installer, but by default they update only the rc channel links and do not take over current:

version=0.16.0-rc1
curl -fsSL "https://github.com/bglenden/casa-rs/releases/download/v${version}/install-casa-rs.sh" \
  | bash -s -- --version "$version"

That creates:

  • ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>
  • ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/rc
  • ~/.local/bin/<command>-rc for each command, such as ~/.local/bin/calibrate-rc

If you want the RC install to become the default suite immediately, add --activate.

docs.title: Put the suite on PATH
docs.text:
The installer links the suite's commands into ~/.local/bin. Add that directory to your shell startup file such as ~/.zshrc:

export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

Reload the shell:

source ~/.zshrc

docs.title: Use Python from the suite
docs.text:
Activate the suite-local virtual environment:

source "$HOME/.local/opt/casa-rs/current/python/bin/activate"
python -c "import casars; print(casars.__version__)"

The suite's Python starts each task's executable from its own suite: in an install at ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>, casars.tasks.gaincal(...) runs ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>/bin/calibrate. To target a different installed suite explicitly, set:

export CASARS_SUITE_ROOT="$HOME/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>"

To run one task from another file, set its override variable, such as CASARS_CALIBRATE_BIN or CASARS_IMAGER_BIN. A wheel installed outside a suite, such as one from PyPI, needs CASARS_SUITE_ROOT (or the task's override) to run tasks; its in-process tools (casars.data.Image, casars.data.Table, casars.tools) need no executables.

The Python executable lookup and protocol-compatibility rules are documented in Python Compatibility.

docs.title: Stable and RC installs
docs.text:
Stable releases and release candidates can live on the same machine at the same time. The installed layout is:

~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>/
  bin/                  (every task executable of the catalog)
  python/               (the suite's virtual environment)
  wheels/
  bundle-manifest.json
~/.local/opt/casa-rs/stable -> ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<stable-version>
~/.local/opt/casa-rs/rc -> ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<rc-version>
~/.local/opt/casa-rs/current -> ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>
~/.local/bin/
  calibrate -> ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/current/bin/calibrate
  calibrate-stable -> ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/stable/bin/calibrate
  calibrate-rc -> ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/rc/bin/calibrate
  ...                   (the same links for each executable in bin/,
                         except feather, immath and impv)

Switch the default suite by repointing ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/current, re-running the installer with --activate, or keep multiple installs in place and choose one explicitly with CASARS_SUITE_ROOT or that suite's Python virtual environment.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
If you are working from a checkout instead of a published release asset, install Rust and build locally:

curl https://sh.rustup.rs -sSf | sh
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
cargo build --release --workspace --bins

A Python package installed from the checkout (pip install -e crates/casars-python) runs the newest debug or release build of each task executable in that checkout's target/ (or $CARGO_TARGET_DIR), unless CASARS_SUITE_ROOT or the task's override is set. A task whose executable is not built names the cargo build -p <package> --bin <executable> that builds it.

To package a local release-style bundle, run:

scripts/build-python-dist.sh dist/python
scripts/package-suite-bundle.sh \
  --version "$(sed -n 's/^version = \"\\(.*\\)\"/\\1/p' Cargo.toml | head -n 1)" \
  --platform "$(scripts/install-suite.sh --print-platform)" \
  --bin-dir target/release \
  --wheel-dir dist/python \
  --out-dir dist/python

To build, bundle, and install the current checkout in one step, run:

just install-local

just install-local runs just install-local-suite. Use --force for an ad-hoc reinstall of the same checkout version:

just install-local -- --force

To install a published release suite without rebuilding the checkout or rerunning release verification gates, run:

just install-release 0.17.0

docs.title: Provider Contracts and Schema Bundles
docs.text:
This document defines the contract model between functionality providers and their consumers:

  • the Python package casars
  • the task executables of the application catalog, run directly from the command line

ADR-0017 makes these the product surfaces; casa-rs has no separate launcher, terminal UI, native GUI, or interactive browser sessions.

The goal is to keep one source of truth for each provider surface while still allowing different transports.

docs.title: Core Rule
docs.text:
The canonical boundary contract is a versioned, typed provider bundle.

  • Providers own request/result, object, and private adapter semantics. The shared catalog owns reusable public parameter concepts.
  • Rust types implement that contract inside the provider.
  • Generated machine artifacts publish that contract to the CLI, Python parity checks, and test fixtures.
  • Presentation hints belong in the same schema bundle as annotations. They do not replace the semantic contract.

JSON and JSON Schema remain valid machine transports and projections. They are not the semantic model itself, and the user-editable parameter profile format is sparse TOML.

The source of truth is therefore not:

  • raw CLI flags
  • hand-maintained Python wrappers
  • an app-local default or alias table

It is the checked catalog plus the self-contained provider schema bundle that embeds the concepts referenced by its surface definition.

docs.title: Surface Kinds
docs.text: A provider bundle advertises one of two surface kinds (ProviderSurfaceKind). Every parameter surface is a task; the profile SurfaceKind has the single variant task.

docs.title: Task Surfaces
docs.text:
Task surfaces are one-shot operations with a request and a result.

Examples:

  • calibrate
  • casars-imager

Machine-facing shape:

  • --protocol-info
  • --json-schema
  • --json-run <SOURCE>

The protocol is request/result oriented. CLI flags and Python wrappers are projections of the same task contract.

A task SurfaceDefinition also binds its public parameter names to the shared ParameterCatalog and adapts the resolved set into the provider's private, idiomatic Rust request.

docs.title: Object Surfaces
docs.text:
Object surfaces expose stateful handles with constructors, properties, methods, and lifecycle operations.

The object surfaces are casars.data.Image and casars.data.Table, and the CASA tool classes of casars.tools (ADR-0019): simulator (CASA's sm), measures (me), quanta (qa), componentlist (cl), image (ia), coordsys (cs), table (tb), msmetadata (msmd) and ms.

The casars.data classes are persistent data access APIs; the casars.tools classes are CASA tools with CASA's method names, parameter order and effective defaults. All are used in-process from Python, are not forced into the task-binary model and have no standalone executable. One bundle, casars_data_objects (casars.data.schema_bundle(), protocol version 1), describes them all; its tool entries all come from one list of the casars.tools classes, and each names its own module in its projection entry (Compatibility). casars.simutil, a port of CASA's simutil helper class rather than a CASA tool, is not an object surface and is not in the bundle.

A CASA tool's entry carries:

  • each method's parameters as a JSON Schema object whose properties give the value kind and the installed CASA binding's default (a parameter without a default is required); CASA's any parameters refer to the shared CasaQuantityArgument and CasaMeasureArgument components, and its record parameters are JSON objects;
  • each method's result kind (a boolean, string, record, list of strings or array of numbers);
  • in projections.python, the tool's module and class and the parameter order of its constructor (keyword-only casa-rs controls) and of each method, which JSON Schema's properties do not keep;
  • in annotations.python, whether casa-rs implements each method.

The Python tests compare each tool's entry with inspect.signature of the class and with the installed CASA binding.

Machine-facing shape:

  • a versioned schema bundle describing constructors, properties, methods, and common value types
  • no standalone executable required

docs.title: Bundle Shape
docs.text:
Each provider surface exposes one canonical schema bundle. The bundle contains at least:

  1. protocol
  2. protocol name
  3. protocol version
  4. surface kind: task or object
  5. semantic contract
  6. tasks: operations with request/result schemas
  7. objects: constructors, properties, methods, lifecycle operations
  8. parameter contract where the surface is parameterized
  9. shared ParameterCatalog concepts
  10. the task SurfaceDefinition
  11. parameter bindings, defaults, roles, validation, migrations, and aliases
  12. shared component schemas
  13. reusable logical value definitions referenced across operations
  14. annotations
  15. labels, descriptions, ordering, groupings, examples, advanced/basic and hidden flags, units, and other presentation metadata
  16. projection metadata where needed
  17. CLI flag names and positional rules
  18. Python parameter names

The semantic layer is authoritative. Annotations and projections may add presentation or mapping metadata, but they must not change semantic meaning.

Task providers use the shared ProviderContractEnvelope<Semantic, Schemas> implementation in casa-provider-contracts. The envelope owns protocol identity, semantic operations, reusable components, annotations, projections, and embedded parameter surfaces. Provider crates supply only their typed domain schemas and operations. The common validator rejects wrong surface kinds, missing parameter surfaces, noncanonical actions, duplicate operations, protocol metadata errors, and semantic/flattened schema drift.

docs.title: Application Catalog and Launching
docs.text:
casa-provider-contracts also owns the single ApplicationCatalog. Every parameter surface has exactly one task-application entry that references the surface by stable ID, and every application is a task: each catalog entry is one task surface. Display name, category, and protocol family are projected from the referenced surface rather than copied into another inventory. Each application adds only executable/package identity (launch), its explicit override variable, the kinds of dataset it reads, and packaging visibility (include_in_suite); an entry carrying any other field is refused. Several surfaces may share one executable, a family whose first word names the surface: imhead and imstat run imexplore; plotms runs msexplore; split runs mstransform; and gaincal, bandpass, applycal, fluxscale, and gencal run calibrate, whose own calibrate surface is its default.

casa_provider_contracts::resolve_task_executable is the one search for the file a task runs; Python reaches it through casars._core. The first step that applies decides:

  1. the task's override variable (override_env, CASARS_<APP>_BIN, such as CASARS_IMAGER_BIN or CASARS_CALIBRATE_BIN);
  2. a suite root, CASARS_SUITE_ROOT or else the installed suite the Python package belongs to (the installer's environment is <suite>/python, beside <suite>/bin and bundle-manifest.json), whose bin/ holds the executable;
  3. a development checkout: the newest debug or release build of the executable under the workspace the package was built from, in $CARGO_TARGET_DIR or target/.

A step that applies but lacks the file is an error naming what it lacked, and never falls through to a later step, so an installed suite never runs a checkout's build. A missing development build is reported with the cargo build -p <package> --bin <executable> that makes it. Nothing is run through cargo, PATH is not searched, and the caller's own path (current_exe) is not consulted. Python, packaging scripts, and the suite inventory all project from this catalog.

docs.title: Parameter Catalog and Surface Definitions
docs.text:
ADR-0006 defines the common parameter model, including the optional current-only profile contract used by simobserve and msconvert.

ParameterCatalog entries describe reusable concepts:

  • stable semantic ID and canonical CASA-facing name
  • value type, normalization, base constraints, semantic equality, and, where applicable, unit dimension
  • semantic role and persistence class
  • meaning and public documentation

A canonical name has one meaning across surfaces. Reuse is by semantic concept, not by matching strings. Two parameters with different meanings must not share a catalog concept even when a legacy CLI happens to spell them alike.

ParameterBinding describes one concept's use on one surface:

  • absent, literal, or pure conditional default
  • required and activation predicates
  • provably narrowing refinements, aliases, and projection metadata
  • an optional context role consistent with the concept's semantic role

Aliases are unique within a surface and cannot shadow any canonical parameter name on that surface.

Concept roles are part of the contract. A path that is safe as an input does not become an output merely because both serialize as strings. Runtime-only controls such as executable overrides, progress paths, telemetry, and Last controls are explicitly non-persistable. There are no run-time confirmations: CASA's own parameters, such as overwrite, are the consent to replace or change data.

A task SurfaceDefinition maps the resolved CASA-named parameter set into a one-shot provider invocation.

Every optional parameter has an explicit default. Conditional defaults depend only on other parameters and form an acyclic graph. Dataset-derived context is an explicit suggestion or override, never an undeclared default.

Semantic evolution is guarded by the append-only fingerprints in resources/parameter-contract-history.json. Changing a concept's type, normalization, constraints, units, role, or persistence requires a new semantic revision. Changing a surface's bindings, defaults, predicates, provider projections, or migrations requires a new surface contract version. Run scripts/check-parameter-contract-history.py --update only after making and reviewing those version bumps; the normal architecture gate is check-only.

docs.title: Sparse Parameter Documents
docs.text:
The human interchange format is versioned sparse TOML. The [casars] table identifies format version, surface ID, surface kind (always task), and contract version. The [parameters] table contains required values and normalized semantic differences from current defaults.

This makes additive evolution cheap: a newly added optional parameter receives its current default without adding an override to a saved file. A surface may publish explicit ordered migrations for older contracts, including warnings for changed defaults. An empty migration set declares a current-only surface: only the exact current contract and canonical parameter names are accepted. The simobserve and msconvert surfaces are current-only. A chain may start after contract 1: tclean, the imager's surface since contract 29, migrates profiles from contract 28, the imager surface's last, and answers to that former id. Future, stale, and otherwise unmigratable contracts are errors.

Parameter documents do not support includes, environment or shell expansion, remote URLs, or executable expressions. Relative task paths resolve against the selected workspace or process current directory, not the profile file's parent. See Task Parameter Profiles for the user contract and managed-state lifecycle.

docs.title: Canonical schema discovery
docs.text:
--json-schema emits a machine representation of the canonical provider bundle, including the parameter catalog and applicable surface definition.

Consumers project from the embedded canonical surface in-process. Providers expose no second schema-discovery action or cached presentation payload.

Every one-shot task binary answers --json-schema, --protocol-info and --json-run <SOURCE> through the shared task front end below, which owns stdin and file ingestion, JSON decoding and encoding, and the typed reply. A binary keeps only its typed execution callback.

docs.title: The shared task front end and typed replies
docs.text:
casa-task-runtime::TaskFrontEnd is the one entry every task binary's main calls, including the family binaries that host several surfaces. A surface's choices take their canonical names (--preset amplitude_vs_time), and every flag it declares, short ones such as msexplore's -o included, reaches its parameter. The front end is generic over the binary's execution callback and owns the surface's declared flags, the base sources, --workspace, --unset, --save-params, --no-save-last, the non-executing --show, --template (also --profile-template), --describe and --validate, and the machine actions. A spelling the surface declares is always its parameter, so imregrid's --template names its template image and --profile-template gives its profile. A family binary's first word names the surface it runs, such as imexplore imstat, mstransform split or calibrate gaincal; the first hosted surface runs otherwise. A --json-run request names its surface itself; the fixed_args that imhead, imstat and the calibration surfaces carry repeat it as the first word, while split and plotms carry none. The callback reads the resolved values into the binary's typed request through TaskInvocation's typed reads, and TaskInvocation::is_set tells a value the run sets from a default. What a command line prints is the callback's text (msexplore's summary in the user's format), with notes such as msexplore's flag-edit line on stderr; --json-run carries the value and result instead.

The binary's main owns the process. It reads the logging configuration from the environment (CasaLoggingConfig::from_env) and passes it, with its arguments, how the process enters a directory (std::env::set_current_dir) and its standard output and error, to TaskFrontEnd::main. The front end reads no environment variable and changes no process state itself (ADR-0016): it applies the logging flags, and for a run installs logging that writes to the stderr it was handed and to a log table only when one is named. An action that runs nothing installs no logging, so a bad CASA_RS_LOG_* setting refuses only a run.

A command-line run enters its workspace (--workspace, the current directory otherwise) before the task starts, as a Python task call starts the executable in its workspace. Every relative path the run names then resolves in the workspace: inputs, products, and paths inside a parameter's text, such as imstat's region file or the image in immoments' mask expression. The files the controls name (--params, --save-params, a log table) are read and written from where the command was run, before it enters. A --json-run runs where its caller started it.

--json-run SOURCE takes a TaskRunRequest, {"surface": ..., "values": {...}} with the CASA-named values the caller set, and resolves it against the surface's contract inside the binary. It writes one TaskReply to stdout:

  • {"status": "succeeded", "surface", "value", "result"}, where value is what CASA's task returns (null for None), kept ahead of the provider's full result, from which products are projected;
  • {"status": "failed", "surface", "kind", "message", "parameter"?}, where kind is validation (refused before anything changed), execution, or interrupted: the task caught an interrupt, stopped at its next safe point and published nothing, as casars-imager does on SIGINT.

The exit status agrees with the reply: 0 for success, 2 for a validation failure, 1 for an execution failure and 130 for an interrupted run. classify_task_exit reads a finished process from its exit status and stdout alone, never stderr, and keeps a launch failure, a signal and a malformed reply distinct from the task's own failures. A provider contract carries both schemas under semantic.front_end.

A surface with a managed_output contract names the decoder that reads its provider result (calibration-report-v1, imager-run-v1, simobserve-run-v1): the reply's result is that result, from which the completion decoder projects products and the summary. Nothing is injected into the binary's arguments to ask for it.

Last has one owner on each path: a command line run of a binary records Last before the callback and Last Successful only after success, unless --no-save-last; --json-run reads and writes neither, so Python task calls save none. Every Python task call is one invocation shape: the executable the resolver names, the surface's fixed_args, then --json-run - with the values the call set on stdin. Python passes the task's log lines to sys.stderr as they arrive and classifies the reply through casars._core. A success returns a TaskCompletion carrying the reply's value and the products the decoder projects. A validation reply raises TaskParameterError, a ValueError whose completion's status is refused; anything else raises TaskExecutionError, whose completion's status is failed, interrupted, signalled or malformed_reply. A value the contract refuses when Python resolves the call raises ValueError before anything starts, or TypeError for a value of the wrong type.

A succeeded reply's value is CASA's return value as a tagged CasaValue (casa-provider-contracts): none, bool, int, float (non-finite values as "nan", "inf" and "-inf"), string, list, an ordered dict whose keys are strings or integers, and typed arrays (bool_array, int_array with dtype int32 or int64, float_array with float32 or float64, complex_array, str_array) that carry their shape and their data in column-major (Fortran) order. casars._core rebuilds Python's types and NumPy arrays from it, so a CASA-signature wrapper returns what CASA returns. tools/casa-compat/record_casa_returns.py records the structure of CASA's own return values (resources/casa-compat/casa-6.7.6.14/returns.json), which the image, MeasurementSet and calibration task tests compare against.

docs.title: Shared Versioned Component Schemas
docs.text:
Protocol-independent basic types have versioned shared schemas, reused across task and object surfaces rather than redefined per provider. Component families include:

  • scalar values
  • bool
  • integer and floating-point values
  • complex values
  • strings
  • array values
  • dtype / primitive type
  • shape
  • axis-order semantics
  • fixed-shape and variable-shape array forms
  • record values
  • named fields with nested values
  • keyword maps
  • table keywords
  • column keywords
  • image misc/info-like nested metadata maps
  • error envelopes
  • stable error code
  • message
  • optional structured details
  • file/path references
  • file path
  • directory path
  • path role hints for validation

These shared schemas are versioned explicitly:

  • a versioned family name for the logical type set
  • stable $defs / component identifiers within that family
  • additive extension within a compatible protocol version
  • explicit protocol-version bumps for breaking shape changes

The logical schema describes semantics, not one transport encoding. For example, Python maps image planes directly to NumPy arrays in-process.

docs.title: Projection Rules
docs.text: All consumers project from the same canonical schema bundle.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
CLI parsing is a projection from the semantic contract plus CLI annotation metadata such as flag names and positional rules.

CLI flags are not the source of truth.

Each task executable's command line, through the shared task front end, also projects the common Defaults, Last, Last Successful, explicit profile, reset (--unset), save (--save-params), and no-save (--no-save-last) source operations, and the non-executing --show, --template, --describe and --validate. Invocation starts from Defaults unless a source is explicit.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Python stays ergonomic and typed, but its wrappers and docs are checked against the canonical schema bundle so signatures and enums cannot drift.

For task surfaces, generated Python callables start the task's executable with the canonical --json-run - transport; Python does not host a second provider protocol engine. For object surfaces, Python binds directly in-process.

casars.parameters exposes the common typed task profile, while generated task-specific wrappers delegate through the same runtime. Python must not keep a second default or migration implementation.

docs.title: Surface inventory
docs.text: Every catalog surface is a task surface; the generated parameter reference lists them. The object surfaces above are not parameter-profile surfaces.

docs.title: Implementation Guidance
docs.text:
• Define typed Rust structs and enums that serialize exactly to the canonical schema bundle shapes.
  • Define reusable catalog concepts once and bind them explicitly on every parameterized task surface.
  • Generate schema output from those types rather than hand-maintaining schema JSON.
  • Keep presentation hints in the schema bundle as annotations.
  • Keep protocol names and protocol versions explicit and machine-checkable.
  • Add CI parity tests so catalog coverage, wrappers, docs, sparse profiles, and projections cannot drift from the canonical schema bundle.

This preserves one source of truth while supporting direct Rust APIs, the Python package, and the task executables.

docs.title: Rust API
docs.text:
The generated Rust API documentation is published alongside this site at:

  • Rust API reference

The rustdoc tree is generated from source documentation comments with cargo doc --workspace --no-deps.

docs.title: Task Parameter Profiles
docs.text:
Truth class: normative user contract Status: implemented Verification: just docs-check; <executable> --help (for example imexplore --help)

casa-rs uses one parameter model for its one-shot tasks. A profile can be loaded by a task executable's command line or manipulated from Python without changing the parameter names or their meaning. Every parameter surface is a task (ADR-0017).

This guide describes the implemented interface from ADR-0006, including current-only surface evolution. Provider JSON requests, results, and progress remain machine transports; TOML is the sole human-authored parameter-profile format.

The generated parameter reference lists every cataloged task surface, its parameters, and their canonical concept revisions, types, units, defaults, groups, and summaries.

docs.title: Sparse TOML format
docs.text:
Parameter profiles are UTF-8 TOML with an ASCII-oriented syntax. They are designed to paste cleanly into Markdown:

[casars]
format = 1
surface = "tclean"
kind = "task"
contract = 30

[parameters]
vis = "data/target.ms"
imagename = "products/target"
imsize = 1024
cell = "0.2arcsec"
field = "target"
spw = "0:32~255"
specmode = "cube"
weighting = "briggs"
niter = 10000
threshold = "2mJy"

Only required values and values that differ semantically from current defaults are written. Resetting a field removes its override and reveals the current default. Quantities are compared by value and dimension, so equivalent values such as "0.001Jy" and "1mJy" do not create a false override.

Files do not execute code. Includes, URL loading, environment expansion, shell expressions, and executable selection are not part of the format. Unknown, duplicate, inactive, or wrong-surface parameters are errors with source locations where possible. A compound value is replaced as one value; profiles are not recursive merge patches.

A surface retains older profiles only when its canonical definition publishes an explicit ordered migration chain; other stale contracts and historical aliases are rejected rather than silently interpreted. The imager surface became CASA's tclean at contract 29: a profile naming surface imager at contract 28, its last, migrates. Its casa-rs names move to CASA's (phasecenter_field to phasecenter, mask_box and mask_image to mask, minor_cycle_length to cycleniter, and dirty_only = true to niter = 0), its values to CASA's forms, and an omitted value whose default changed (imsize, cell, cycleniter, nterms) takes tclean's with a warning. Older imager contracts are refused.

Contract 30 changes casa-rs's keyword-only write_pb extra to default to True, so an ordinary tclean call writes the .pb product CASA writes. This changes none of CASA's 92 parameters or their defaults; pbcor=False still leaves the restored image uncorrected. A contract-29 profile with write_pb omitted adopts the new default with a warning. An explicit write_pb=False remains an opt-out. The owner approved this change on 2026-10-31 (#980).

Relative dataset and product paths resolve against the explicit workspace or the process current directory. They do not resolve relative to the profile file merely because the file lives elsewhere.

docs.title: Native EVLA AW convolution functions
docs.text:
With gridder = "awproject", aw_cf_source = "casa-import" is the default and requires an explicit cfcache input directory. CASA CFS_/WTCFS_ cells are imported read-only; auto does not select or create a cache.

Select aw_cf_source = "native-evla" to use the frozen homogeneous 25 m EVLA dish model without CASA at runtime. Supply evla_surface (the explicit dish surface input file), native_cf_cache (a separate private cache directory), native_cf_working_size, native_cf_oversampling, native_cf_cache_bytes, and native_cf_maximum_cells. Sampling and resource bounds are explicit request parameters, not inferred from a cache's contents. The native cache is not CASA-readable and cannot also be supplied as cfcache.

native_cf_policy defaults to "reuse-only": an incomplete or invalid cache fails without generation. "generate-missing" creates absent cells and retains valid completed cells; corruption remains an error. "regenerate" explicitly replaces all requested cells. Neither source falls back to the other. These parameters are available through the same CLI flags, task JSON, sparse profiles, and generated Python wrapper. Profiles store the requested paths/action/bounds, not compiled plans, generated cells, cache inventory, or publication state. This exposes the frozen EVLA case, not general telescope support.

The native cells follow tclean's terms as CASA's AWProjectFT reads them: aterm, psterm, wbawp (cells at each window's frequency, or at the image reference frequency alone; without the aperture CASA drops it), conjbeams (the weight cell's conjugate beam) and wprojplanes (one plane is co-planar). An imported CASA cache already holds the cells its run made; with it only conjbeams changes the run, choosing the cell each sample grids with.

docs.title: Sources and precedence
docs.text:
Every task run resolves its parameters from exactly one base source:

  • Defaults
  • Last attempted
  • Last successful
  • an explicit profile file

Resolution order is:

current defaults
  -> one base source
  -> explicit CLI or Python overrides

Dataset-derived suggestions are explicit values, not hidden defaults. Choosing another base source replaces the base rather than merging into it.

Command-line and Python calls start from Defaults unless a source is specified. A missing managed profile is distinct from an unreadable or invalid one: asking for Last when no Last file exists is reported as missing, and a present corrupt Last file is reported as an error and is never silently replaced by Defaults.

docs.title: Managed Last files
docs.text:
By default, managed state lives under the workspace:

<workspace>/.casa-rs/parameters/<surface-id>/last.toml
<workspace>/.casa-rs/parameters/<surface-id>/last-successful.toml

Last records command-line runs. Last attempted is saved after resolution and validation, immediately before execution. Last successful changes only after a successful result. Cancellation or failure leaves Last successful unchanged. --no-save-last skips both writes for one run.

A Python task call saves neither file; reading an existing Last (parameters.last(...)) and writing one explicitly (TaskParameters.write_last()) remain available. A task executable's --json-run, the path Python's calls take, reads and writes no Last either. Last therefore has one owner: the task front end, for a command-line run of a task executable.

casa-task-runtime::ParameterRuntime owns source resolution and managed Last persistence; the CLI and Python projections call that boundary rather than keeping their own Last-state logic.

Set CASA_RS_STATE_DIR to redirect managed state in automation. This changes the state location, not the workspace used for relative task paths.

Automatic Last updates never overwrite an explicit profile file.

docs.title: CLI contract
docs.text:
Each task runs from its own executable, which the application catalog names (calibrate, imexplore, casars-imager, simobserve, ...). Every task executable runs on the shared task front end in casa-task-runtime, so all take the same command line; --help prints it with the surface's parameters.

<executable> [SURFACE] [SOURCE] [OVERRIDES] [CONTROLS]
<executable> [SURFACE] --show [SOURCE] [OVERRIDES] [--save-params FILE]
<executable> [SURFACE] --template | --profile-template | --describe [NAME] | --validate FILE
<executable> --json-run <SOURCE> | --json-schema | --protocol-info
  • SURFACE is the first word of a family executable, which hosts several surfaces: calibrate (calibrate, applycal, gaincal, bandpass, fluxscale, gencal), imexplore (imhead, imstat), msexplore (msexplore, plotms) and mstransform (mstransform, split). Without it the first hosted surface runs. Other executables host one surface.
  • SOURCE is exactly one of --defaults (the default), --last, --last-successful or --params FILE.
  • OVERRIDES are the flags the surface declares, or --unset NAME, which removes an override.
  • CONTROLS are --workspace DIR (where relative paths resolve and Last and Last Successful live), --save-params FILE (also write the run's resolved sparse profile) and --no-save-last.

For example:

calibrate gaincal --ms ngc5921.ms --out ngc5921.G0 --refant VA15 --solint inf
imexplore imstat --last --show --save-params imstat.toml

The non-executing actions resolve the same sources and overrides and run nothing: --show prints the resolved parameters, and with --save-params FILE saves them as a sparse profile; --template writes a documented example with defaults and units in comments, whose commented defaults are not active overrides; --describe [NAME] describes the surface or one parameter; --validate FILE checks a profile against the surface. Overrides use the generated CLI flag spellings listed in the generated parameter reference, or the parameter's own name, such as --vis or --threshold; some surfaces declare their own spellings, such as calibrate's --ms and --out.

A list's command-line form is comma-separated (--archivefiles a.exp,b.exp). A flag repeated for a list without a fixed size adds to it, so --archivefile a.exp --archivefile b.exp names both archives; any other repeated flag takes its last value. A path list given as one string, on the command line, in a profile or in a --json-run request, is split at its commas before each path is normalized, so every route names the same paths. A refused value names its parameter, on the command line as in a reply's parameter.

There are no run-time confirmations. CASA's own parameters are the consent: overwrite=true replaces a product, and a task that changes data in place does so, as in CASA. Where CASA guards a change, casa-rs does too, for example applycal and flagdata saving the flags to a new flag version first (flagbackup, default on). No task takes a confirmation flag.

The machine actions (--protocol-info, --json-schema, --json-run) are the same on every task executable; --json-run gives a typed reply (provider contracts). A spelling the surface declares is always its parameter: imregrid's --template is its template image, so there --profile-template writes the profile. A run started from a task's command line enters its --workspace first, so its relative paths resolve there, as they do for a Python call in its workspace.

docs.title: Python contract
docs.text:
The Python API exposes the same profile model:

from casars import parameters, tasks

p = parameters.defaults("tclean", workspace="project")
p.update(
    vis="data/target.ms",
    imagename="products/target",
    imsize=1024,
    cell="0.2arcsec",
)
p.save("profiles/target-imaging.toml")

result = p.run()                          # in the draft's workspace
result = tasks.run("tclean", p, niter=0)  # the draft, with one more value

Companion constructors are parameters.last(...), parameters.last_successful(...), and parameters.load(path, ...). TaskParameters supports mapping-style updates, reset(name), reload(), save(path), provider_invocation(), and run(**values). As a mapping, a draft holds the parameters that have a value, so a loaded profile runs through a CASA-named wrapper, in the current directory, as tasks.gaincal(**parameters.load(path)). The invocation exposes the provider protocol name/version, the arguments (the surface's fixed arguments, then --json-run -), and the exact canonical request stdin.

tasks.run(task, parameters=None, /, *, workspace=None, **values) accepts every catalog task. It starts from the draft, or Defaults, sets values, and runs in workspace: the draft's, or the current directory. The CASA-named wrappers take the surface's parameters and run in the current directory. Each call starts the task's own executable, found by the resolver (Install), with --json-run -, and passes its log lines to sys.stderr as they arrive. The log reaches stderr at the logging configuration's threshold, WARN by default; CASA_RS_LOG_STDERR_PRIORITY=INFO also shows a task's INFO lines, such as its start and completion. Ctrl-C (KeyboardInterrupt) is passed to the task as SIGINT; the task has ten seconds to stop before it is killed, and the KeyboardInterrupt is then raised again.

A value the contract refuses, such as a parameter its gridder does not read, raises ValueError before anything starts, or TypeError when the value has the wrong type. A task that refuses its parameters itself, such as an input that does not exist, raises casars.tasks.TaskParameterError, a ValueError; one that starts and does not succeed raises casars.tasks.TaskExecutionError, a RuntimeError. Both carry the .completion, whose status is refused, failed, interrupted, signalled or malformed_reply, with its message and the parameter it names. TaskBinaryNotFoundError, a FileNotFoundError, says what the resolver lacked; TaskInvocationError means the executable could not be started, and TaskResultError that a success's result was malformed. tasks.run returns a TaskCompletion with the command run, its workspace, returncode, stdout (the reply), stderr (the log), the provider_invocation, CASA's return value from the reply, and the declared products (result, products); result projection remains Rust-owned.

The CASA-named wrappers and their type stubs are generated from the catalog, under casars.tasks; there is no second provider-specific task API. A surface that names its CASA task (casa_task; every surface but the casa-rs tasks calibrate, msexplore and msconvert, and plotms) has CASA's exact signature: CASA's parameters in CASA's order, positional or by keyword, with CASA's defaults, then casa-rs's own controls, keyword-only. Its wrapper returns CASA's value: imstat's statistics dictionary with NumPy arrays, immath's True, flagdata's summary dictionary in summary mode and {} in its other modes, flagmanager's version list in list mode, gaincal's and bandpass's tables and selected data, fluxscale's flux densities, None for most tasks. A parameter casa-rs does not implement yet is taken only at CASA's default and refused at any other value, naming its issue; the wrapper's docstring lists them. The other wrappers take keyword arguments and return the TaskCompletion. CASA compatibility compares each surface with its CASA task.

docs.title: What profiles intentionally exclude
docs.text:
• casars.data.Image and casars.data.Table object-handle lifecycle
  • progress files, executable overrides, Last controls, and telemetry
  • saved region and mask mutations, which are dataset artifacts
  • an exact resolved historical replay record

If exact run replay is needed, record a separate run manifest containing the fully resolved invocation and versions. A sparse profile records user intent under the current contract and defaults.

docs.title: ADR-0006: Unified parameter catalog and sparse profiles
docs.text:
Status: accepted Date: 2026-07-09 Truth class: normative Supersedes: Superseded by: ADR-0017, in part (session surfaces, session Last handling and the TUI and GUI consumers were removed on 2026-10-20; the parameter catalog and sparse task profiles stand)

Amended: 2026-11-02, on owner approval. This record now also holds the current-only profile contracts (decided 2026-09-03, #551) and the surviving rule of the provider schema bundle decision (2026-04-19); their separate records were deleted and git history keeps them. Text that ADR-0017 superseded is removed.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Task defaults, aliases, validation, command-line parsers, Python signatures and saved requests drift apart when each consumer defines its own parameters. Users need parameter files that are readable in a Markdown code block, easy to edit and review, sparse enough to adopt newly added defaults, and usable from a task's command line and from Python without changing meaning.

docs.title: One catalog; the bundle is a projection
docs.text:
The repository maintains one checked aggregate catalog. Its authoritative concepts are:

  • ParameterCatalog: reusable parameter concepts with stable semantic IDs, canonical CASA-facing names, value types, units or dimensions, normalization, semantic roles, persistence classes, constraints, and documentation.
  • SurfaceParameterBinding: a surface-specific use of a catalog concept, including its default, requirement and activation rules, narrowing constraints, aliases, presentation hints, and private provider projection.
  • SurfaceDefinition: a task definition containing the ordered bindings, the migrations and the provider projection that surface needs.

Each provider's versioned schema bundle is the machine boundary between the provider and its consumers. It embeds the catalog concepts and surface definitions it uses and is generated from them. The bundle must not become a second source of truth: CLI parsers, JSON Schema and Python signatures are views derived from it, and no consumer hand-defines a default, alias, shape or behaviour that the catalog does not carry.

A canonical name has one meaning. imsize keeps the same value semantics wherever it is bound. Parameters that share a spelling but differ in meaning use different semantic IDs and are never silently unified; such a binding carries a reviewed_homonym record citing this ADR. Roles such as input, output, selection, science control and presentation stay explicit, so a path or scalar cannot be reused in an unsafe role because its storage type matches.

Task definitions resolve parameters into one-shot invocation requests. Tool objects (ADR-0019), runtime controls and transient state are not parameterized surfaces.

docs.title: Sparse TOML profiles
docs.text:
Human parameter documents use sparse TOML. The metadata table identifies the document format, logical surface, surface kind and contract version; the parameters table holds required values and semantic differences from the current defaults. Optional values equal to their defaults are omitted.

[casars]
format = 1
surface = "tclean"
kind = "task"
contract = 29

[parameters]
vis = "data/target.ms"
imagename = "products/target"
imsize = 1024
cell = "0.2arcsec"
niter = 10000
threshold = "2mJy"

Evolution rules:

  • Adding an optional defaulted parameter does not require existing files to change.
  • An omitted parameter adopts the current default. Loading warns when a migration lists that default as changed since the document's contract.
  • Renames and type or value changes use explicit ordered migrations of the sparse overrides, each advancing one contract version. A chain may start after contract 1; a profile older than its first migration is refused (tclean migrates contract 28 to 29 and refuses older profiles). A renamed surface keeps its former ids, which a saved profile may still name (imager, now tclean).
  • A newly required parameter needs a migration or causes a load error.
  • Future document or contract versions are rejected.
  • Saving rewrites a document at the current contract version against the current defaults.

docs.title: Current-only surfaces
docs.text: A surface declares a current-only profile contract by publishing an empty migration set. Such a surface accepts exactly its current contract version, exposes and accepts only canonical names with no compatibility aliases, rejects stale and future contract versions instead of interpreting or rewriting them, and serializes only required values and non-default overrides whose persistence class is profile. Omitted optional values adopt the current defaults; they are not materialized to preserve an older contract's behaviour. Shipped profiles, tutorials and examples advance with the contract. simobserve and msconvert are current-only; the other surfaces keep ordered migration chains.

docs.title: Managed Last state
docs.text:
The managed workspace store is:

<workspace>/.casa-rs/parameters/<surface-id>/
  last.toml
  last-successful.toml

CASA_RS_STATE_DIR may redirect the managed state root for automation without changing how relative task paths resolve. Managed writes use a per-surface lock, a same-directory temporary file and atomic replacement.

last.toml records the validated resolved intent of a command-line run immediately before execution; last-successful.toml updates only after successful completion. Failure or cancellation does not replace the successful state. --json-run, which Python's task calls use, reads and writes no Last (ADR-0017 item 4).

casa-task-runtime is the sole owner of these rules: source parsing, resolution, attempted-state capture, managed persistence and completion. Task executables and the Python package delegate to it and keep no alternate lifecycle maps, Last writers or test-only persistence paths.

Opening an explicit profile never grants permission to overwrite that file. Automatic persistence always targets the managed store; changing an explicit file needs an explicit save.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive: - defaults, validation, docs, projections and persistence share one source of truth - sparse files stay readable and naturally adopt additive parameters - a profile has the same meaning on a task's command line and in Python - task aliases keep distinct logical identities and Last files even when they share a provider binary - a current-only surface's meaning is its one canonical request vocabulary

Negative: - every parameterized surface defines complete typed bindings, and migrations unless it is current-only - default changes need deliberate compatibility diagnostics - a contract bump of a current-only surface deliberately invalidates profiles that were not updated

Neutral / tradeoffs: - sparse profiles reproduce user intent under current defaults; they are not exact historical run-replay records - provider bundles may use JSON as a machine transport, but JSON Schema and CLI flags are projections rather than the semantic model

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
1. Persist complete JSON request envelopes, freezing old defaults into every file.
